Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: 27-year-old male with acute onset profuse watery diarrhoea (hourly), crampy abdominal pain (6/10), nausea/vomiting (milk-related), subjective fever, mild oliguria. Brother has similar illness. No blood in stool. Otherwise healthy.  

Working diagnosis: Acute viral gastroenteritis (likely norovirus). Supported by abrupt onset, watery stools, family member affected, self-limited course expected (DDx likelihood High).  

Considerations:  
• Acute bacterial gastroenteritis/food-borne infection (Medium likelihood)—would consider if symptoms persist >48 h or worsen.  
• Transient post-infective lactose intolerance (Low–Medium)—milk triggers vomiting.  

Management:  
• Oral rehydration therapy—advise OTC Dioralyte; emphasize frequent small sips.  
• Symptomatic control—paracetamol for pain/fever.  
• Dietary advice—clear fluids, bland soft foods (soup, mashed foods); avoid dairy/alcohol until recovery.  
• Red flags discussed—return if unable to tolerate fluids, persistent fever, blood in stool, worsening pain, symptoms >48 h.  
• Follow-up telehealth in 1–2 days or sooner if deterioration.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – High likelihood: Sudden profuse watery diarrhoea, family member affected, nausea/vomiting, self-limiting pattern.  
2. Acute bacterial gastroenteritis – Medium likelihood: Similar symptoms; possible takeaway food source; will consider if no improvement or if systemic features develop.  
3. Transient lactose intolerance – Low–Medium likelihood: Milk precipitates vomiting; may be secondary to mucosal injury from infection.
